articles.title: Your First 48 Hours in Chengdu
articles.excerpt: A calm, first-timer-friendly route through pandas, teahouses, old lanes, and the everyday rhythm that makes Chengdu memorable.
articles.bodyMarkdown:
## Start with pace, not a checklist

Chengdu rewards a slower rhythm. For a first visit, choose **one anchor experience per half-day** and leave space for tea, food, and unplanned neighborhood walks. Your first 48 hours should help you understand the city rather than race across it.

## Day one: pandas, parks, and a relaxed evening

Begin early if the panda base is important to you. Conditions, opening arrangements, and transport details can change, so check the venue's current official information before leaving. Later, return to the city for a park or teahouse. People's Park is frequently included in public accounts of English-language Chengdu tours, but the real value is the contrast between a major attraction and ordinary city life.

For the evening, keep the plan flexible. A Sichuan opera performance can add cultural context, while a neighborhood dinner gives you time to ask practical questions about spice levels and local dishes.

## Day two: historic Chengdu and a guide-led theme

Choose a compact group of city sights rather than crossing Chengdu repeatedly. Kuanzhai Alley and Wenshu Monastery are commonly referenced in the public guiding sources reviewed by MeetChengdu. Pair them with one theme that matters to you: food, tea culture, architecture, photography, or contemporary city life.

## When a local English guide helps most

A guide is most useful when you want interpretation, not just transport. Before committing, ask about the exact meeting point, duration, route, language level, credentials where relevant, included costs, cancellation terms, and how payment is handled. MeetChengdu does not process bookings; contact happens on the linked source platform.

> Every guide profile on this site is compiled from public evidence and may be unclaimed. Verify identity and current service details directly before making arrangements.

## Practical final check

Keep venue addresses in Chinese, allow extra transfer time, and avoid building a day around too many distant districts. A good Chengdu introduction should leave you curious, not exhausted.

## A directory, not a booking marketplace

MeetChengdu helps English-speaking travelers discover public evidence about potential local guides. We do not take payment, promise availability, or present unclaimed profiles as endorsements.

## Our evidence ladder

We prefer a direct public post or profile that clearly connects a person with English-language guiding in Chengdu. Independent media coverage can strengthen a profile when it names the person and describes relevant experience. A platform search result without a confirmed profile is treated as a lead and labeled accordingly.

We do **not** copy private contact details, infer personal information, reproduce customer comments as testimonials, or invent ratings. Search snippets that cannot be reliably attributed are not presented as confirmed facts.

## Confidence is expressed in words

A profile may include strong, moderate, or limited public evidence. The source cards on each profile explain what was observed and when it was last reviewed. Evidence of past guiding does not prove current availability, licensing status, price, insurance, or service quality.

## Corrections and removal

The person shown, an authorized representative, or a reader with evidence can use the Claim / Correct / Remove form. Requests are reviewed by an administrator. We may update wording, add evidence, mark a profile as claimed after verification, or remove the public listing.

## What travelers should verify

Confirm identity on the destination platform, ask for current credentials where relevant, agree on itinerary and fees in writing, and understand cancellation and payment arrangements. Never send sensitive identity documents through an unverified channel.

## Begin with the day you want

Instead of searching for the “best” guide, define the experience you want help interpreting. A tea-focused morning, a food walk, a classic-sights introduction, and a western Sichuan extension require different knowledge and pacing.

## Tea culture and everyday Chengdu

If you want parks, teahouses, and neighborhood conversation, look for public evidence that mentions those settings—not simply a broad “city tour” label. Ask whether the guide can explain etiquette, ordering, and the social role of tea without turning the visit into a scripted stop.

## Food without assumptions

Tell a guide about allergies, dietary restrictions, and your comfort with spice before the day begins. Ask whether tasting costs are included and whether the route can adapt. Public content can suggest an interest in food, but only a direct conversation can confirm the actual itinerary.

## Classic sights for a first visit

For pandas, Kuanzhai Alley, Wenshu Monastery, or Sichuan opera, use the source cards to see which topics have appeared in a guide's public work. This is evidence of a connection, not a quality score.

## Longer routes

Jiuzhaigou and western Sichuan involve more planning than a city walk. Confirm transport, permits or venue requirements where applicable, overnight arrangements, weather contingencies, and who is responsible for each booking.

articles.title: Chengdu Panda Base: A Simple Visitor's Guide (2026)
articles.excerpt: What the Chengdu Panda Base is, what you'll see there, and the few practical steps — passport booking, an early start, the sightseeing bus — that make the visit easy.
articles.bodyMarkdown:
## What the Panda Base is

The Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding — almost everyone just calls it the Panda Base — is a breeding and research centre in the north of Chengdu that is also open to visitors. It was founded in 1987 with six giant pandas rescued from the wild, and has since grown into one of the largest captive-breeding centres in the world, home to well over a hundred giant pandas today.

It doesn't feel like a city zoo. The grounds are large, green and hilly, with bamboo groves, lakes and spacious outdoor enclosures, and you can easily spend a whole morning walking between them. For many visitors it is the highlight of a trip to Chengdu.

![View across the green, hilly grounds of the Chengdu Panda Base](/images/panda-base-grounds.webp)

*The base is large, green and hilly. Photo: [MspreilsCN](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:A_distant_view_in_Panda_Base.jpg), [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0), via Wikimedia Commons.*

## What you'll see

![Three giant pandas eating bamboo together at the Chengdu Panda Base](/images/panda-base-bamboo.webp)

*Giant pandas spend much of the morning eating bamboo. Photo: [Enricoroberto5](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Panda_giganti_al_Giant_Panda_Breeding_Research_Base_Chengdu.jpg), [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0), via Wikimedia Commons.*

- **Adult giant pandas** in outdoor enclosures and "villas", eating bamboo, climbing and — very often — sleeping.
- **Subadult pandas**, the young pandas that are usually the most playful to watch.
- **Nursery houses** (such as the Sun and Star nurseries), where the base's youngest pandas are shown in season. Whether newborn cubs are on display depends on the time of year.
- **Red pandas**, which are smaller, fox-like and far more active than giant pandas. Their area is a favourite with children.
- **Panda Creek Valley** and other landscaped areas, plus exhibition spaces about panda biology and conservation.

![Three red pandas play-fighting on the grass at the Chengdu Panda Base](/images/panda-base-red-pandas.webp)

*Red pandas are much livelier than giant pandas. Photo: [MSK](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:3_red_pandas_play-fighting.jpg), [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0), via Wikimedia Commons.*

Signs along the main routes are in Chinese and English, and the paths are easy to follow.

## The best time to go

Go in the **morning**, as early as you can. Pandas are most active around feeding time, roughly from opening until about 10:00. By late morning many have eaten and fallen asleep, often high up in a tree, and in summer the afternoon heat makes them even less active.

![A giant panda asleep on a wooden platform at the Chengdu Panda Base](/images/panda-base-sleeping.webp)

*By late morning, many pandas are asleep. Photo: [Colin W](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Panda_at_the_Chengdu_Research_Base_of_Giant_Panda_Breeding,_Chengdu_-_panoramio.jpg), [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0), via Wikimedia Commons.*

Weekdays are noticeably calmer than weekends. Chinese public holidays — especially the October Golden Week and the Spring Festival — are the busiest days of the year.

Plan on **three to four hours** for an unhurried visit.

## Tickets and booking with a passport

The base now works on advance, real-name booking. In 2026:

- **Book in advance.** Use the base's official WeChat mini program or official account (成都大熊猫繁育研究基地), or an authorised platform. Trip.com is the one most often recommended for visitors without a Chinese phone number. Bookings open up to 14 days ahead; one to three days is usually enough on weekdays, but book one to two weeks ahead for weekends and holidays.
- **Choose "passport" as your ID type.** Your ticket is tied to your passport number.
- **Bring the original passport.** It is checked at the entrance, and a photo or photocopy may not be accepted.
- **Price.** Several 2026 sources list adult admission at about **CNY 55**, with discounts for some students, children and seniors. Confirm the current price when you book.
- **Don't count on buying at the gate.** Some sources say tickets are only sold online; others say a window sometimes sells leftover tickets. Booking ahead avoids the problem.

Tickets are sold for **morning** or **afternoon** sessions, and you can't enter before your session starts. Recent booking guides list these times (they can change by season, so check the time on your booking):

| Season | Morning entry | Afternoon entry | Closes |
|---|---|---|---|
| March–October | 7:30–12:00 | 12:00–17:00 | 18:00 |
| November–February | 8:00–12:00 | 12:00–16:30 | 17:30 |

Book the morning session and aim to arrive shortly before it opens.

## Getting there

The base is in Chenghua District, in the north of the city. Keep the address in Chinese on your phone to show a driver:

**成都大熊猫繁育研究基地，成都市成华区熊猫大道1375号**
(Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding, 1375 Panda Avenue, Chenghua District)

- **Taxi or ride-hailing (DiDi):** the easiest option for an early start, usually 30–45 minutes from the city centre depending on traffic.
- **Metro and shuttle:** Metro Line 3 serves the area, with a panda shuttle bus from the metro. Station names differ between sources, so check the current route in your map app before you set off.

There are two main visitor entrances, the **South Gate** and the **West Gate**. The South Gate is the usual choice for a first visit; the West Gate is often described as a quieter start. Either works, as long as your driver knows which one you want.

![A visitor entrance to the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding](/images/panda-base-entrance.webp)

*One of the base's visitor entrances. Photo: [Kreisverkehrsampel](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Chengdu_Research_Base_Eingang.jpg), [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0), via Wikimedia Commons.*

## Getting around inside

The base is big and hilly, so wear comfortable shoes. An official **sightseeing bus** loops between the South and West Gates, stopping at the main panda areas. The base lists:

- **CNY 30 per person** for visitors over 1.3 m; children 6 and under, or under 1.3 m, ride free.
- Running **7:30–17:30** (March–October) and **8:00–17:00** (November–February).
- Tickets through the official mini program or account, or on site on the day.

A good pattern is to walk to the nearest enclosures first while the pandas are active, then take the bus to cross the park.

## A few practical tips

- **Bring water and a light snack**, especially in summer. There are shops inside, but they can be far apart.
- **Be quiet and don't use flash.** The pandas are easily disturbed, and staff will remind you.
- **Rain isn't a problem.** Pandas don't mind it, and a light drizzle often thins the crowds. Bring an umbrella or raincoat.
- **Finish by lunchtime.** After a morning with the pandas, the rest of the day suits something slower — a teahouse in People's Park, for example. [Your First 48 Hours in Chengdu](/blog/first-48-hours-in-chengdu) shows how to fit the base into a relaxed first day.

## Before you go

- [ ] Morning session booked under your **passport** number.
- [ ] Original passport packed.
- [ ] Gate chosen (south or west), and the Chinese address saved for the driver.
- [ ] Taxi or DiDi planned to arrive before your session opens.
- [ ] Rules re-checked on the official WeChat account or your booking platform the day before.

## Sources

- Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding — Wikipedia (founding in 1987 with six rescued pandas): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chengdu_Research_Base_of_Giant_Panda_Breeding
- Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding, official English site (address, tourism hotline): https://www.panda.org.cn/en/
- Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding, Sightseeing Bus Service (CNY 30, hours, routes, purchase channels): https://m.panda.org.cn/en/service/sightseeingbus/
- TripChina.me, "Chengdu Panda Base Tickets: How Foreigners Can Book Online" (updated 11 Oct 2026; passport option, verification lanes, sessions): https://tripchina.me/how-to-book-chengdu-panda-base-tickets/
- China Survival Kit, "Chengdu Panda Base 2026" (updated 8 Oct 2026; price, 14-day window, advance booking, Golden Week): https://chinasurvivalkit.com/blog/chengdu-panda-base-guide
- RealChinaTrip, "Chengdu Panda Base in 2026" (south vs west gate, original passport, early arrival): https://realchinatrip.com/blogs/city-guide/panda-base-tickets-guide-panda-base-guide-tickets-best-time-2026-updated-rct
- ChinaTripedia, Panda Base ticket and opening hours (transport options): https://chinatripedia.com/chengdu-research-base-of-giant-panda-breeding-ticket-opening-hours-highlights-and-tips/
- Cover photo: young giant panda by [George Lu](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Panda_in_Chengdu_Research_Base_of_Giant_Panda_Breeding_-_7708872342.jpg), [CC BY 2.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0), via Wikimedia Commons.

articles.title: Visiting Sanxingdui from Chengdu: A Simple Guide (2026)
articles.excerpt: The bronze masks of Sanxingdui are one of China's great archaeological mysteries, and they're only 20 minutes from Chengdu by train. Here's how to book, get there and make sense of what you see.
articles.bodyMarkdown:
## What Sanxingdui is

Sanxingdui (三星堆, "Three Star Mounds") is an archaeological site in Guanghan, just north of Chengdu, and the museum built beside it is one of the most remarkable in China. In 1986, farmers and archaeologists uncovered two pits filled with more than a thousand objects — huge bronze masks with protruding eyes, a life-size bronze figure, bronze "sacred trees", gold foil, jade and elephant tusks — left by a Bronze Age culture that flourished here roughly 3,000 years ago.

What makes Sanxingdui so striking is how *different* it looks. These faces don't resemble anything else from ancient China, and the culture left no writing that has been deciphered, so much of what the objects meant is still debated. Between 2020 and 2023, six more pits were excavated, adding gold masks, new bronzes and ivory carvings, and in July 2023 a large new museum building opened to show them.

If you have an extra day in Chengdu, this is one of the best ways to spend it.

![A bronze head with large stylised eyes from Sanxingdui](/images/sanxingdui-bronze-heads.webp)

*Bronze heads like this one are among the most striking finds. Photo: [Gary Todd](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Ancient_Bronze_Mask_from_Sanxingdui_1.jpg), [CC0](http://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/deed.en), via Wikimedia Commons.*

## What you'll see

The museum has two connected buildings, and most visitors walk through both:

- **The new Comprehensive Museum** tells the story chronologically, from the site's discovery to the newest finds from the 2020–2023 excavations. Plan on two hours or more.
- **The Bronze Museum** focuses on the most famous ritual bronzes. Allow about an hour.

Highlights to look out for:

- **The Bronze Standing Figure** — about 2.6 metres tall including its base, often described as the oldest life-size bronze human figure in the world.

![The upper body of the Bronze Standing Figure at Sanxingdui, with its oversized hands](/images/sanxingdui-standing-figure.webp)

*The Bronze Standing Figure, with its huge hands that once held something now lost. Photo: [Gary Todd](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bronze_Colossal_Standing_Figure,_Sanxingdui_b.jpg), [CC0](http://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/deed.en), via Wikimedia Commons.*
- **The masks with protruding eyes** — the largest is well over a metre wide, with cylindrical eyes jutting out from the face. They're the image most people associate with Sanxingdui.
- **Bronze Sacred Tree No. 1** — nearly four metres tall, with birds perched on its branches.

![Birds perched on the branches of a bronze sacred tree at Sanxingdui](/images/sanxingdui-sacred-tree.webp)

*Birds on the branches of a bronze sacred tree. Photo: [Gary Todd](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bronze_Tree,_Sanxingdui_1c.jpg), [CC0](http://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/deed.en), via Wikimedia Commons.*
- **The gold masks**, including the half-mask from Pit 5 found in the recent excavations, the largest Shang-era gold mask yet discovered in China.

![A gold mask on display at the Sanxingdui Museum](/images/sanxingdui-gold-mask.webp)

*One of Sanxingdui's gold masks. Photo: [Thoslee](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Sanxingdui_Gold_Mask.jpg), [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0), via Wikimedia Commons.*

Signs are in Chinese and English, but the labels are short. Because there are no written records from this culture, the objects need interpreting more than most museum pieces — reading up beforehand, or going with someone who can explain them, makes a big difference.

## Tickets and booking with a passport

- **Price:** 72 RMB for general admission.
- **Book in advance.** Tickets are sold by date and time slot (morning and afternoon, plus evening slots on some dates), and weekends, public holidays and school breaks sell out. Book a few days ahead; for holidays, book as early as the system allows.
- **Where to book:** the museum's official website (sxd.cn) or its official WeChat mini program ("三星堆博物馆"), which accept passports according to a September 2026 test of the booking process. If the official channels give you trouble, Trip.com and Klook also sell tickets to foreign visitors.
- **Bring your original passport.** It's scanned at the entrance, and a photo or copy may not be accepted.

Don't plan on buying a ticket at the gate.

## Opening hours

- **08:30–18:00**, with the last entry at **17:00**.
- On some dates (public holidays and in January, February, July and August) the museum may stay open until 20:00.
- It closes only on Chinese New Year's Eve.

Hours and slots can change, so check the time on your booking.

## Getting there from Chengdu

Sanxingdui is in Guanghan, about 40 km north of central Chengdu.

- **High-speed train + bus or taxi (best):** trains from Chengdu East (some also from other Chengdu stations) reach **Guanghan North** in about 20 minutes. From the station, **bus No. 13** runs to the museum, or a taxi covers the 7 km in about 15 minutes for roughly 20 RMB. In busy periods the taxi queue at Guanghan North can be long, so the bus is often quicker.
- **Taxi or DiDi from Chengdu:** about an hour each way, roughly 150–200 RMB. Easiest with a group or children.
- **Tourist buses:** direct buses from Chengdu take 70–90 minutes; schedules vary.

Keep the name in Chinese on your phone: **三星堆博物馆，四川省广汉市** (Sanxingdui Museum, Guanghan, Sichuan).

## How long to spend, and when to go

Plan on **three to four hours** inside, plus travel. A comfortable day looks like this: an early train, arriving for the 08:30 opening; the main halls before the late-morning crowds (busiest roughly 10:30–14:30); lunch in Guanghan or near the museum; and back in Chengdu by mid-afternoon.

Weekdays are noticeably quieter than weekends.

## A few tips

- **Read a little first.** Even ten minutes on the 1986 and 2020–2023 discoveries makes the masks far more interesting.
- **Start with the new building** for the story, then finish in the Bronze Museum.
- **Wear comfortable shoes.** The two buildings are large and there's a lot of walking.
- **Pair it with something calm.** After a morning of bronzes, an evening teahouse back in Chengdu is a good balance. [Your First 48 Hours in Chengdu](/blog/first-48-hours-in-chengdu) has ideas, and the [Chengdu Panda Base guide](/blog/chengdu-panda-base-guide) covers the city's other must-see day.

If you'd like English commentary inside the museum, our [directory of English-speaking guides in Chengdu](/guides) lists guides whose public posts mention Sanxingdui. Check credentials and prices with them directly.

## Before you go

- [ ] Ticket booked for your date and time slot, under your **passport** number.
- [ ] Original passport packed.
- [ ] Train to Guanghan North booked (or a car arranged), arriving before your slot.
- [ ] Museum name saved in Chinese for the taxi or bus.
- [ ] Booking time re-checked the day before.

## Sources

- Real Chengdu, "Booking Tickets to Sanxingdui Museum as a Foreign Tourist: I Tested the Official Booking Process" (23 Sep 2026; official channels, passport entry, 72 RMB, hours, time slots, closure day): https://realchengdu.com/en/article/how-do-i-buy-tickets-through-the-sanxingdui-museums-official-channels
- Wander in China, "Sanxingdui Museum 2026" (25 Feb 2026; museum layout, highlights and dimensions, time needed, transport options, crowds): https://www.wanderinchina.com/destinations/chengdu/sanxingdui-museum-guide/
- China Highlights, "Sanxingdui Museum: How to Visit from Chengdu" (train to Guanghan North, bus No. 13, taxi): https://www.chinahighlights.com/chengdu/attraction/sanxingdui-museum-in-guanghan.htm
- Gov.cn, "New Sanxingdui Museum building starts trial operation" (July 2023; more than 1,500 relics on display): https://english.www.gov.cn/news/202307/28/content_WS64c31938c6d0868f4e8de257.html
- Wikipedia, "Sanxingdui Museum" (background on the 1986 pits): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanxingdui_Museum
- Cover photo: bronze mask with protruding eyes by [Gary Todd](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Ancient_Bronze_Mask_from_Sanxingdui_with_Protruding_Eyes_%26_Ears_a.jpg), [CC0](http://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/deed.en), via Wikimedia Commons.

articles.bodyMarkdown:
## Start with what you need help with

Most visitors who look for a guide in Chengdu aren't really looking for transport. Taxis and ride-hailing apps cover that. What they want is interpretation: someone who can explain a panda's daily routine, the social rules of a teahouse, or why a 3,000-year-old bronze mask matters, and who can order dinner without guessing at the spice level.

So before you look at anyone, write one sentence describing the day you want. "A relaxed morning at the panda base and an afternoon in a park teahouse" is a very different brief from "two days in Jiuzhaigou with train transfers." The first needs a good explainer. The second needs someone who handles logistics, hotels and weather plans. That sentence will tell you which questions matter most.

## Know what "licensed" means in China

In China, guiding is a regulated job. Paid guides are expected to hold a national tour-guide qualification and be registered with a travel agency or guide-service organisation. The registration gives them an operational guide certificate. Industry write-ups describe paid guiding without one as unlicensed ("black guide") work, which leaves travelers with little recourse if something goes wrong.

The practical part for travelers is newer. On 30 June 2025, the Ministry of Culture and Tourism introduced a 2025 version of the electronic guide certificate and a physical **guide identity card**. According to the ministry's notice and Chinese press coverage:

- The card is vertical and colour-coded by grade: green (junior), blue (intermediate), orange (senior), red (special grade).
- The front shows the guide's photo, name, grade, certificate number, and **guiding language**.
- The back shows the registering organisation, the managing authority, the validity period, and a **QR code that travelers can scan** to check the electronic certificate.
- Old-style cards were valid alongside the new ones until 31 December 2025 and lapsed from 1 January 2026.

So in 2026 you can reasonably ask a guide to show the newer card, and you can scan its QR code yourself. A professional guide expects this and won't take offence. (The verification page may open in WeChat rather than an ordinary browser. If you can't open it, ask the guide to show their electronic certificate on their own phone.)

A licence is not the only sign of a good guide. Some useful companions, such as interpreters, students or friends of friends, aren't licensed guides and don't claim to be. That can be fine for an informal city walk. It matters more when someone is selling a multi-day itinerary, collecting money for tickets and hotels, or taking you somewhere remote.

## Read public evidence the way an editor would

Many English-speaking guides in Chengdu market themselves on Xiaohongshu (RedNote), a Chinese platform most visitors never browse. That's why MeetChengdu compiles public profiles in English. Each profile on this site links back to its original source, and none of them is a recommendation.

When you look at any guide's public presence, these signals carry weight:

- **Specific, dated posts from real guiding days.** Recurring posts from one place are stronger evidence than a polished bio. [Fiona](/guides/fiona) posts near-daily from the Chengdu Panda Base, including morning queue reports from the west gate. [Laura](/guides/laura) keeps a dated work diary of family and small-group tours.
- **Credentials stated in the guide's own words.** [Libby](/guides/libby) lists an English degree, TEM-8 certification, an English tour-guide licence and four years guiding foreign visitors in Chengdu. [Betty](/guides/betty) lists an English tour-guide licence and certification as a bilingual docent at the panda base.
- **Language evidence, not just claims.** [Charles](/guides/charles) writes most of his posts in English, covering Jiuzhaigou, Huanglong and Chengdu's museums. Seeing how someone writes or speaks in English is more useful than a "fluent English" line.
- **A clear specialism.** [Jenny](/guides/jenny) advertises English commentary at the Sanxingdui Museum. [Tommy](/guides/tommy) describes himself as a licensed English-speaking guide and posts about Qingcheng Mountain, Dujiangyan, Leshan and teahouse and mahjong sessions.

Every one of these is a statement the person made in public, not something we've checked in person. Several profiles also show screenshotted thank-you notes from clients. Treat those as marketing material: they may be genuine, but you can't verify them.

## Questions to settle before you agree

A short written exchange protects both sides. Ask for:

1. **Identity and credentials.** Their name as it appears on the guide card, and a photo of the card's front if they hold one. Scan the QR code when you meet.
2. **The exact plan.** Meeting point (in Chinese characters), start and finish times, and the order of stops.
3. **What the price includes.** Guide fee, car and driver, fuel and parking, entrance tickets, sightseeing buses, meals, train fares. Agencies' own published ranges for a private guide in Chengdu run from roughly US$75 to US$450 a day, depending on hours, transport and group size. Those are sellers' figures, so get your own quote.
4. **Who books what.** Panda base, Sanxingdui and many other sites need real-name advance booking with your passport details. Agree whether you book or they do, and never send a passport photo through a channel you haven't verified.
5. **Payment and cancellation.** When payment is due, by what method, and what happens if it rains, a site closes, or you get sick.
6. **No-shopping terms.** If you don't want shop stops, say so in writing.
7. **Insurance and responsibility,** especially for mountain, high-altitude or multi-day trips.

## Red flags

- They won't say who they're registered with, or the name keeps changing.
- They want full payment up front for a short city day, through an unfamiliar link.
- The price is far below what similar services advertise, and there's a vague mention of "stops."
- The public profile has no dated posts from guiding days, only reposted scenery.
- They pressure you to decide quickly or to move the conversation to a private channel straight away.

None of these proves bad intent, but each one is a good reason to slow down.

## How to use this directory

Start from [the guide directory](/guides) and filter by the experience you wrote down at the beginning: pandas, tea culture, city classics or western Sichuan. Our earlier piece on [choosing a guide by interest](/blog/tea-food-and-neighborhoods-chengdu) explains why that works better than chasing the "best" guide. If this is your first visit, [Your First 48 Hours in Chengdu](/blog/first-48-hours-in-chengdu) shows where a guide adds the most.

MeetChengdu doesn't book, take payment or vouch for anyone. When you click through to a source, the conversation is yours.

## Before you book

- [ ] I've written down the experience I want, and the guide's public posts match it.
- [ ] I've seen the guide card or credential in a form I can check, and I'll scan the QR code on the day.
- [ ] The route, hours, meeting point and **everything the price includes** are in writing.
- [ ] I know who books timed or real-name tickets, and I haven't sent ID documents through an unverified channel.
- [ ] Payment method, deposit and cancellation terms are agreed.
- [ ] I understand that this site's profiles are compiled from public evidence, may be unclaimed, and are not endorsements.

> Every guide profile on this site is compiled from public evidence and may be unclaimed. Verify identity, credentials and current prices directly with the guide before making any arrangement.

## Sources

- Ministry of Culture and Tourism (General Office), notice on launching the 2025 electronic guide certificate and guide identity card: https://zwgk.mct.gov.cn/zfxxgkml/scgl/202506/t20250613_960565.html
- People's Daily, "2025版电子导游证及导游身份标识卡6月30日启用" (card design, colours, QR verification, transition to 31 Dec 2025): http://ent.people.com.cn/n1/2025/0613/c1012-40500284.html
- CCTV News, same announcement: https://news.cctv.com/2025/06/13/ARTIes8K8JU8DbRDwsKxuDsT250613.shtml
- Travel China With Me, "Is My Guide Certified? Decoding the China Tour Guide License" (agency registration, "black guide" terminology): https://travelchinawith.me/china-facts/china-tour-guide-license/
- QuietRoutes, Chengdu private tour guide page (updated 20 Sep 2026; published range USD 75–450 / RMB 500–3,000 per day): https://quietroutes.com/travel-guide/chengdu-private-tour-guide/
- HeroGuide, English tour guide in Chengdu (2026 edition; published US$90–220 half day, US$160–380 full day, excluding tickets): https://www.hero-guide.com/chengdu-guide/english
- Guide descriptions: MeetChengdu profiles (scripts/seed-data.json; source cards last reviewed October 2026) for fiona, laura, libby, betty, charles, jenny, tommy.

articles.bodyMarkdown:
## Why Chengdu

Chengdu, the capital of Sichuan province, is best known for giant pandas and fiery Sichuan food, but what most visitors remember is its pace. It's a huge, modern city that still makes time for tea in the park, long lunches and games of mahjong. It's also the gateway to some of western China's most spectacular sights: the Leshan Giant Buddha, the Bronze Age masks of Sanxingdui, the ancient irrigation system at Dujiangyan, and the lakes of Jiuzhaigou.

This page is our starting point for planning a trip. Each section gives you the essentials and links to a detailed guide.

## When to go

Spring (March to May) and autumn (September to November) are the most comfortable times to visit, with mild temperatures and fewer very hot or wet days. October and November tend to be the driest months. Summer is hot and humid, and winter is cool and damp, but neither is a reason to stay away: pandas are often more active on cool mornings.

Avoid Chinese public holidays if you can, especially the October Golden Week and the Spring Festival. Sights, trains and hotels are at their busiest then, and popular attractions sell out.

## How many days do you need?

- **2 days:** the Panda Base, a park teahouse, the old lanes and a hot pot dinner. Our [First 48 Hours in Chengdu](/blog/first-48-hours-in-chengdu) shows how to pace it.
- **3–4 days:** add one or two day trips: Sanxingdui, Leshan or Dujiangyan.
- **5 days or more:** add a slower day in the city, a cooking class or teahouse afternoon, and consider an overnight trip to Jiuzhaigou or western Sichuan.

## Getting there

Chengdu has **two airports**:

- **Tianfu International (TFU)**, the newer and larger one, about 50 km south-east of the centre. Metro Line 18 runs to Chengdu South Railway Station in about 35 minutes; change to Line 1 for the centre.
- **Shuangliu International (CTU)**, closer to the city (about 17 km). Metro Line 10 connects it to the network.

Check which airport your flight uses before you book a hotel or a transfer. Chengdu is also well connected by high-speed rail to Chongqing, Xi'an and other cities.

**Visas:** citizens of many countries can use China's **240-hour visa-free transit** policy through Chengdu's airports, staying up to 10 days in Chengdu and ten other Sichuan cities (including Leshan and Deyang, where Sanxingdui is) if they're travelling on to a third country with a confirmed onward ticket. The list of eligible countries changes, so check the official rules for your nationality before you travel.

## What to see in Chengdu

- **The Chengdu Panda Base.** The visit most people plan their trip around. Book ahead with your passport and go in the morning, when the pandas are most active. Full guide: [Chengdu Panda Base: A Simple Visitor's Guide](/blog/chengdu-panda-base-guide).
- **People's Park and its teahouses.** The best place to see everyday Chengdu: tea, card games, dancing and the famous matchmaking corner.
- **The old lanes.** Kuanzhai Alley and Jinli are busy and touristy but fun, especially in the evening. Wenshu Monastery is a calmer, working Buddhist temple nearby.
- **Du Fu Thatched Cottage and Wuhou Shrine.** Two of the city's best historic sites, for Tang poetry and Three Kingdoms history.

## Food, tea and evenings

Sichuan food is more than chilli. Expect numbing Sichuan pepper, sour and sweet flavours, and plenty of dishes that aren't spicy at all. Try hot pot at least once, and ask for a milder broth if you're unsure.

Tea culture is a big part of daily life here. Our guide to [tea, food and neighbourhoods](/blog/tea-food-and-neighborhoods-chengdu) explains how to choose experiences by interest. For evenings, see [After sunset fun in Chengdu](/blog/after-sunset-fun-in-chengdu).

## Day trips from Chengdu

- **Sanxingdui.** Extraordinary Bronze Age masks and figures, 20 minutes away by high-speed train. Full guide: [Visiting Sanxingdui from Chengdu](/blog/sanxingdui-from-chengdu).
- **Leshan Giant Buddha.** The world's largest ancient stone Buddha, carved into a cliff above the river. It's a classic day trip; many visitors combine it with Mount Emei over two days.
- **Dujiangyan and Qingcheng Mountain.** A 2,000-year-old irrigation system that still works, paired with one of the birthplaces of Taoism.
- **Jiuzhaigou and Huanglong.** Turquoise lakes and travertine terraces in the mountains north of Chengdu. Too far for a day trip; plan at least two nights.

## Getting around and paying

- **Metro:** Chengdu's metro is extensive, cheap and signposted in English. It's the easiest way to cross the city.
- **Taxis and ride-hailing:** DiDi is widely used. Keep your destination written in Chinese on your phone to show drivers.
- **Paying:** Alipay and WeChat Pay are used almost everywhere, and both let international visitors link a foreign Visa or Mastercard. Set them up before you arrive, and carry some cash as a backup. A small fee may apply to larger foreign-card payments.
- **Booking attractions:** many sites, including the Panda Base and Sanxingdui, require advance, real-name booking with your passport, and you'll need the original passport at the gate.

## Finding an English-speaking local guide

You don't need a guide to enjoy Chengdu, but a good one adds context: which panda is which, what the Sanxingdui masks might mean, how to order in a local restaurant, and how to get the most out of a day trip.

- Read [How to Hire an English-Speaking Guide in Chengdu](/blog/how-to-hire-english-speaking-guide-chengdu) for how to check China's official guide ID card and what to agree in writing.
- Browse our [directory of English-speaking guides in Chengdu](/guides), compiled from their public profiles. You can filter by interest: [pandas](/guides?tag=pandas), [tea culture](/guides?tag=tea-culture), [city classics](/guides?tag=city-classics) and [western Sichuan](/guides?tag=western-sichuan).

MeetChengdu doesn't book or take payment; you contact guides directly. Always check identity, credentials and price yourself.

## Quick checklist

- [ ] Visa or visa-free transit eligibility checked for your nationality.
- [ ] Alipay or WeChat Pay set up with a foreign card; some cash as a backup.
- [ ] Panda Base and Sanxingdui tickets booked with your passport.
- [ ] Your hotel address and key destinations saved in Chinese.
- [ ] Airport (TFU or CTU) confirmed and transfer planned.

## Sources

- National Immigration Administration, visa-free transit policies (updated 20 Aug 2026): https://en.nia.gov.cn/n147418/n147463/c183412/content.html
- Travel China Guide, 240-hour visa-free transit in Chengdu (both airports; Sichuan cities covered): https://www.travelchinaguide.com/package/chengdu/144hour-visa-free.htm
- China Highlights, best time to visit Chengdu: https://www.chinahighlights.com/chengdu/best-time-to-visit.htm
- Travel China Guide, best time to visit Chengdu (March–May, September–November): https://www.travelchinaguide.com/cityguides/sichuan/chengdu/best-time-to-visit.htm
- TripChina.me, Chengdu airport to city: CTU vs TFU (2026): https://tripchina.me/chengdu-airport-to-city-transport-guide/
- RealChinaTrip, official 2026 WeChat Pay & Alipay guide for foreigners: https://realchinatrip.com/blogs/payments-apps/china-payment-guide-for-foreigners-2026
